--- title: "How big should the spoon be?" description: "A correctly drawn five hundred beats a biased forty thousand. In a simulated country where the true result is fixed before anyone is interviewed, 500 interviews drawn from the whole register name the winner in 99.2% of runs and 40,000 drawn only from phone owners name it in none of them. Nasir El-Rufai dismissed Nigeria's 2023 polls for the wrong reason, and had the right one in his next sentence." date: 2026-08-16 categories: - stats-in-life engine: knitr # Static listing thumbnail. The post's own figure is plotly and interactive, # so it cannot serve as one; this is built by _thumbnail.R from the same # simulation, and that script carries the post's guards so the two cannot drift. image: thumbnail.png image-alt: "Four sampling distributions. Two sit on the true value, one broad and one narrow; two more sit together a long way to the right of it, the narrowest of all drawn from forty thousand interviews." --- A poll interviews two thousand people and reports a number for a country of ninety million. The objection writes itself: two thousand is a rounding error against ninety million, so how can it say anything? Accuracy comes from the absolute size of the sample, not from the fraction of the population it covers. For a proportion $p$ estimated from $n$ people drawn at random, $$SE = \sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}}$$ in which $N$ does not appear. It enters once, through the finite population correction: $$SE_{\text{fpc}} = \sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}} \times \sqrt{\frac{N-n}{N-1}}$$ That second square root is population size's entire contribution, and it bites only when $n$ is a serious fraction of $N$: $n$ buys precision, not $n/N$. So say Freedman, Pisani and Purves, on chance errors in sampling. That is the half people argue about. The half that decides elections is whether the spoon reached the whole pot, which no arithmetic on a poll that already missed can settle. So this ends in an invented country, where the answer is fixed before anyone is interviewed. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(plotly) comma <- function(x, digits = 0) { formatC(x, format = "f", big.mark = ",", digits = digits) } z <- qnorm(0.975) # 95% two-sided ``` ::: ## The translation ::: {.dual} ::: {.spine} The standard error describes variance around $\mathbb{E}[\hat p]$, not the distance from $\hat p$ to $p$. If the frame excludes part of the population then $\mathbb{E}[\hat p] \neq p$, and that gap is unaffected by $n$. ::: ::: {.dub} A cook tasting soup needs no bigger spoon for a bigger pot, so long as the pot is stirred. Stirring is the assumption, and the one that breaks. If the spoon only reaches the top, a bigger spoon reads the top more precisely and never touches the bottom. The comparison is George Gallup's. ::: ::: ## The claim On 4 February 2023, three weeks before Nigeria voted, Nasir El-Rufai appeared on TVC's *Journalists' Hangout* and [dismissed the opinion polls](https://guardian.ng/news/el-rufai-debunks-obis-election-win-predictions-calls-opinion-polls-a-joke/) that showed Peter Obi ahead: > Opinion polls are distorted... When you have about a 100 million registered > voters and you are sampling 2,000 registered voters or 300 registered voters, > your results from day one are unreliable; they will have high margins of > error. He was right that the polls were wrong. Obi finished third. He said two other things in the same appearance, one about method: > Most of these polls, like the one by Bloomberg, ANAP and the one by Okonjo > Iweala, all used telephone. What percentage of registered voters have phone > numbers in INEC's records? We have found out and it's 31 per cent. and one about his own numbers: > We have done a poll with a sample of nearly 40,000 across Nigeria and the > result of the poll shows that we are ahead. The poll he named is real and published, which makes it usable here. ANAP Foundation and NOIPolls interviewed two thousand registered voters by mobile phone in early February 2023, publishing the sample size and method with the numbers. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # ---- Quoted inputs. Every other number in this post derives from these. ---- # ANAP Foundation / NOIPolls, February 2023; see the method note below. anap_n <- 2000 poll <- c(Obi = 21, Tinubu = 13, Atiku = 10, Kwankwaso = 3, Undecided = 23, Refused = 30) elrufai_n <- 40000 # his own poll, as he described it on air phone_share <- 0.31 # his figure for phone coverage, not checked against INEC # INEC, 2023 presidential election. registered <- 93469008 votes_cast <- 24965218 votes_valid <- 24025940 votes <- c(Obi = 6101533, Tinubu = 8794726, Atiku = 6984520, Kwankwaso = 1496687) # A mistyped input should fail the render rather than publish quietly. stopifnot( sum(poll) == 100, sum(votes) <= votes_valid, votes_valid <= votes_cast, votes_cast <= registered ) ``` ::: Fifty-three of every hundred respondents were undecided or would not say, so the headline numbers do not sum to anything like a vote share. Comparing with the result means rebasing onto the respondents who named a candidate. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} decided <- sum(poll[names(votes)]) poll_obi <- poll[["Obi"]] / decided act_obi <- votes[["Obi"]] / votes_valid miss <- poll_obi - act_obi data.frame( candidate = names(votes), polled = sprintf("%.0f%%", poll[names(votes)]), rebased = sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * poll[names(votes)] / decided), actual = sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * votes / votes_valid) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` candidate polled rebased actual 1 Obi 21% 44.68% 25.40% 2 Tinubu 13% 27.66% 36.61% 3 Atiku 10% 21.28% 29.07% 4 Kwankwaso 3% 6.38% 6.23% ``` ::: ::: Rebased, the poll put Obi on 44.68% of decided respondents. He took 25.40% of valid votes. The gap is 19.29 percentage points, the largest error in the table by a distance. ## What the objection is worth The objection was about the ratio of two thousand to a hundred million. That ratio has exactly one place to enter the arithmetic, so it can be priced. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fpc <- sqrt((registered - anap_n) / (registered - 1)) se_anap <- sqrt(poll_obi * (1 - poll_obi) / anap_n) c(correction = sprintf("%.7f", fpc), se_ignoring_pop = sprintf("%.4f pp", 100 * se_anap), se_including_pop = sprintf("%.4f pp", 100 * se_anap * fpc), shrinkage = sprintf("%.4f%%", 100 * (1 - fpc))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` correction se_ignoring_pop se_including_pop shrinkage "0.9999893" "1.1117 pp" "1.1117 pp" "0.0011%" ``` ::: ::: The correction is 0.9999893. Knowing the population is 93,469,008 rather than unlimited improves the poll's standard error by 0.0011% of itself. That is the whole effect of population size here, and the entire content of the objection. ## The size of the miss The margin of error says how far the estimate would wander if you ran the poll again. The miss is how far it was from the answer. One in units of the other says whether sample size is a plausible explanation. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # The sample size at which the margin of error would have been as wide as the # miss, i.e. the only n for which the objection lands. n_cross <- ceiling(z^2 * poll_obi * (1 - poll_obi) / miss^2) c(miss = sprintf("%.2f pp", 100 * miss), miss_in_se = sprintf("%.1f", miss / se_anap), n_for_margin = comma(n_cross), times_smaller = sprintf("%.0f", anap_n / n_cross)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` miss miss_in_se n_for_margin times_smaller "19.29 pp" "17.3" "26" "77" ``` ::: ::: The miss was 17.3 standard errors. Sampling noise does not produce that: three is already a one-in-a-few-hundred event, and this is nearly six times further out. Solve the margin of error backwards for the sample size that would cover it and you get 26 people, 77 times *smaller* than the poll run. For "your sample was too small" to explain it, the poll would have had to be a group chat. The complaint points the opposite way to the error. Which is the point about his second sentence. The 31 per cent is about the frame, not the sample, and a frame missing two thirds of the register is the one objection on the table that no increase in $n$ can answer. He had the correct argument, and it went unquoted. ## A country where we know the answer Everything above works backwards, pricing the objection against a miss after the fact. It cannot check whether the method *finds* the right answer, because in the real case the result was the only truth available and it arrived three weeks late. So here is a country where the truth is fixed first. NaijaSim has ninety million registered voters, six zones of two states each, and four parties named after colours so that nothing reads as a claim about a person. The zone names are real and nothing else is. One thing is borrowed, the one the argument turns on: phone coverage is his 31%. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(20260817) sim_party <- c("Green", "Blue", "Red", "Yellow") sim_zone <- c("North West", "North East", "North Central", "South West", "South East", "South South") sim_reg_z <- c(21, 12, 15, 18, 9, 15) * 1e6 # registered voters, by zone names(sim_reg_z) <- sim_zone # The national result, set by fiat. Blue wins. sim_target <- c(Green = 0.30, Blue = 0.38, Red = 0.24, Yellow = 0.08) # Zone shares are chosen, EXCEPT North Central, solved so the register-weighted # truth lands exactly on sim_target. sim_zs <- rbind( c(0.08, 0.50, 0.36, 0.06), c(0.10, 0.52, 0.32, 0.06), c(NA, NA, NA, NA ), c(0.34, 0.34, 0.22, 0.10), c(0.72, 0.12, 0.08, 0.08), c(0.48, 0.26, 0.16, 0.10) ) dimnames(sim_zs) <- list(sim_zone, sim_party) i_nc <- match("North Central", sim_zone) sim_zs[i_nc, ] <- (sum(sim_reg_z) * sim_target - colSums(sim_zs[-i_nc, ] * sim_reg_z[-i_nc])) / sim_reg_z[i_nc] # Phone reach is chosen, EXCEPT South South, solved so national coverage is # exactly the 31 per cent he quoted. The poorest zones reach fewest. sim_reach_z <- c(`North West` = 0.160, `North East` = 0.120, `North Central` = 0.300, `South West` = 0.500, `South East` = 0.440, `South South` = NA)[sim_zone] i_ss <- match("South South", sim_zone) sim_reach_z[i_ss] <- (phone_share * sum(sim_reg_z) - sum((sim_reg_z * sim_reach_z)[-i_ss])) / sim_reg_z[i_ss] # Each zone splits 60/40 into two states leaning opposite ways, so no stratum is # internally uniform. B moves 1.5x as far as A, preserving the zone average; the # 0.5 cap keeps every state inside (0, 1). sim_st <- NULL; sim_reg_s <- numeric(0); sim_szone <- character(0) for (zn in sim_zone) { g <- sim_zs[zn, "Green"]; b <- sim_zs[zn, "Blue"] d <- 0.5 * min(g / 1.5, b) s_a <- sim_zs[zn, ]; s_a["Green"] <- g + d; s_a["Blue"] <- b - d s_b <- sim_zs[zn, ]; s_b["Green"] <- g - 1.5 * d; s_b["Blue"] <- b + 1.5 * d sim_st <- rbind(sim_st, s_a, s_b) sim_reg_s <- c(sim_reg_s, 0.60 * sim_reg_z[[zn]], 0.40 * sim_reg_z[[zn]]) sim_szone <- c(sim_szone, zn, zn) } sim_frame_s <- sim_reg_s * unname(sim_reach_z[sim_szone]) # A mistyped country should fail the render rather than publish quietly. stopifnot( sum(sim_reg_z) == 90e6, all(abs(rowSums(sim_st) - 1) < 1e-12), all(sim_st > 0), all(sim_st < 1), isTRUE(all.equal(colSums(sim_st * sim_reg_s) / sum(sim_reg_s), sim_target)), isTRUE(all.equal(sum(sim_frame_s) / sum(sim_reg_s), phone_share)) ) sim_w_true <- sim_reg_s / sum(sim_reg_s) # a fair poll's weights sim_w_frame <- sim_frame_s / sum(sim_frame_s) # what a phone poll actually gets sim_truth <- colSums(sim_st * sim_w_true) sim_ptruth <- colSums(sim_st * sim_w_frame) sim_frame_N <- sum(sim_frame_s) data.frame( party = sim_party, whole_register = sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * sim_truth), phone_frame_only = sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * sim_ptruth) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` party whole_register phone_frame_only 1 Green 30.00% 37.02% 2 Blue 38.00% 33.47% 3 Red 24.00% 20.81% 4 Yellow 8.00% 8.71% ``` ::: ::: Blue wins NaijaSim by 8 points, the fact a poll is being asked to find. The second column is the same country seen through a telephone. Reach is not uniform across zones and the zones do not vote alike, so the 27,900,000 voters who can be called are not a small copy of the 90,000,000 who cannot: among them Green leads by 3.54 points. Phone owners within a state vote like their neighbours here, so all of that gap is geography. Now run the poll: stratified by state, four thousand repetitions at each setting, the register sampled at six sizes down to the 26 the inversion produced and the phone frame at the two that were quoted. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Seeded here, not left to the chunk above, so these numbers do not depend on # how many draws the country construction happened to consume. set.seed(20260817) # Largest remainder: proportional shares rounded the obvious way do not sum to n. sim_alloc <- function(n, w) { raw <- n * w; a <- floor(raw); k <- n - sum(a) if (k > 0) { j <- order(raw - a, decreasing = TRUE)[seq_len(k)]; a[j] <- a[j] + 1 } stopifnot(sum(a) == n) a } SIM_REPS <- 4000 # One rmultinom call per state, vectorised over all 4,000 repetitions. sim_run <- function(n, w) { a <- sim_alloc(n, w) est <- matrix(0, SIM_REPS, 4, dimnames = list(NULL, sim_party)) for (i in seq_along(a)) { if (a[i] == 0) next est <- est + w[i] * t(rmultinom(SIM_REPS, a[i], sim_st[i, ])) / a[i] } est } # "Right" means Blue tops the poll, not merely Blue ahead of Green. sim_summ <- function(est) { g <- 100 * est[, "Green"] c(green = mean(g), sd = sd(g), right = 100 * mean(sim_party[max.col(est, ties.method = "first")] == "Blue")) } # 100.0% is also what 99.95% prints as, so the prose quotes counts, derived here. sim_wrong <- function(pct_right) round(SIM_REPS * (100 - pct_right) / 100) sim_ns_fair <- c(n_cross, 100, 250, 500, 1000, anap_n) sim_ns_phone <- c(anap_n, elrufai_n) sim_fair <- lapply(sim_ns_fair, sim_run, w = sim_w_true) sim_phone <- lapply(sim_ns_phone, sim_run, w = sim_w_frame) sim_ft <- t(sapply(sim_fair, sim_summ)) sim_pt <- t(sapply(sim_phone, sim_summ)) # Indexed by value, not position, so the prose survives a reordered ladder. i_win <- match(500, sim_ns_fair) # the rung the argument turns on i_2k <- match(anap_n, sim_ns_fair) j_2k <- match(anap_n, sim_ns_phone) j_40k <- match(elrufai_n, sim_ns_phone) data.frame( drawn_from = rep(c("whole register", "phone frame"), c(length(sim_ns_fair), length(sim_ns_phone))), interviews = comma(c(sim_ns_fair, sim_ns_phone)), green_says = sprintf("%.2f%%", c(sim_ft[, "green"], sim_pt[, "green"])), wobble = sprintf("%.2f pp", c(sim_ft[, "sd"], sim_pt[, "sd"])), winner_right = sprintf("%.1f%%", c(sim_ft[, "right"], sim_pt[, "right"])) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` drawn_from interviews green_says wobble winner_right 1 whole register 26 30.17% 7.82 pp 64.1% 2 whole register 100 30.06% 4.04 pp 84.8% 3 whole register 250 29.98% 2.50 pp 96.5% 4 whole register 500 29.98% 1.78 pp 99.2% 5 whole register 1,000 30.00% 1.27 pp 100.0% 6 whole register 2,000 30.01% 0.87 pp 100.0% 7 phone frame 2,000 37.02% 0.96 pp 1.5% 8 phone frame 40,000 37.01% 0.21 pp 0.0% ``` ::: ::: Read the last column. 500 interviews drawn from the whole register name the winner in 3,967 of 4,000 runs. 40,000 drawn from the phone frame name it in 0. The winning poll is 80 times smaller, and wins on where its sample came from, not how big it was. The ladder fills in the shape. Even 26 interviews, the group chat from two sections ago, get the winner right 64.1% of the time. The phone frame never climbs: 2,000 interviews pick the wrong winner 3,941 times out of 4,000, and twenty times the interviewing leaves that at 4,000. Meanwhile the wobble column does what the formula at the top promises: the scatter falls with the square root of the sample size. Every bit of precision the phone frame buys is spent stating the wrong answer more firmly. ::: {.cell} ::: {#fig-naijasim .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` Where the poll lands over four thousand repetitions. Drawn from the whole register it sits on the truth, loosely at five hundred interviews and tightly at two thousand. Drawn from the phone frame it sits seven points away, and forty thousand interviews sit in the same wrong place with the least scatter on the chart. Each curve is scaled to its own peak. ::: ::: The shape of the failure is the point. "Unreliable" is normally taken to mean wide. The phone poll at 2,000 scatters 0.96 of a point against the fair poll's 0.87 at the same sample size, and the 40,000 curve is the narrowest on the chart. Width is not what is wrong with them: they are in the wrong place, and the arithmetic that governs width says nothing about position. ::: {.aside-box .hommie} > Dem ask 500 people and dem sabi? The other one ask 40,000 o. Yes, and the five hundred got it right, the forty thousand wrong, every time. Forty thousand is a bigger spoon, not a longer one: if it never reaches past the top of the pot, the extra size only buys the wrong answer to more decimal places. ::: One aside, because it cuts against the original complaint from a second direction. The observed scatter at 2,000 interviews is 0.87 of a point, against the simple-random formula's 1.02. Stratifying by state removes the between-state variation, so the poll's method is slightly *more* precise than the textbook number it was attacked with. ::: {.callout-note} ## Where the numbers come from **Quoted, not derived.** The El-Rufai quotations are as reported by [The Guardian Nigeria](https://guardian.ng/news/el-rufai-debunks-obis-election-win-predictions-calls-opinion-polls-a-joke/) from *Journalists' Hangout* on TVC News, 4 February 2023. The sample size, phone-based stratified random method and the six percentages come from [ANAP Foundation's press release](https://www.anapfoundation.com/press-releases/2023-elections-peter-obi-maintains-lead-amongst-presidential-poll-respondents); the register, votes and candidate totals are INEC's, via the [published breakdown](https://dailypost.ng/2023/03/01/2023-elections-breakdown-of-results-as-tinubu-defeats-atiku-obi/). Outlets differ on the second figure in that first quotation, The Guardian having "300" where [The Cable](https://www.thecable.ng/noi-poll-weve-been-using-same-methodology-since-2015-anap-foundation-replies-critics/) reports "three thousand"; the arithmetic uses ANAP's published 2,000, so nothing turns on it. His own 40,000-sample poll has no published methodology I could find, and appears here as a sample size and nothing else. **Attribution, split deliberately.** That accuracy depends on absolute sample size rather than on the sampling fraction is standard, and Freedman, Pisani and Purves develop it in the chapter on chance errors in sampling in *Statistics*. The soup-and-spoon comparison is attributed to [George Gallup](https://nrich.maths.org/13895), not to them, because I could not verify that the book uses the soup wording. **NaijaSim is invented, and deliberately not a model of Nigeria.** Its zone names are real; its register, zone splits, parties and result are made up. Verifiable zone-level figures for 2023 from a single authoritative source do not exist, and inventing them while calling them the past would be worse than inventing a country and saying so. Only its coverage figure of 31% and three sample sizes come from the real case: 2,000, 40,000, and the 26 the inversion produced. It is seeded, so the figures reproduce exactly. ::: ## What this does not show Four things are doing real work, and several of them cut against the post. **The poll was wrong.** Nothing above defends its finding. It defends its sample size, which is a different object. A poll can be built correctly at the scale it claims and still land 17.3 standard errors from the answer, and this one did. **The 53% who did not answer are carrying the argument.** Rebasing onto decided respondents assumes the silent half would have split like the vocal half. That is the largest assumption on this page, and it is plainly false. A different assumption moves 44.68% a long way. **The 31 per cent is his figure, not a verified one.** It is quoted as his claim about INEC's records and used only to size an illustration. If true coverage is higher the frame problem is smaller than the simulation implies, though it would have to be very much higher to stop being the better objection. **NaijaSim's coverage gap was set to a size that flips the winner.** That is the honest limit of it. Different reach figures produce a phone frame that gets the answer right, and I chose ones that do not. It shows a coverage gap of the size he described is *sufficient* to produce a confident wrong answer that more interviewing cannot fix, not that this happened to the ANAP poll. It also assumes phone owners within a state vote like their neighbours, when real bias runs by age and income too; that everyone answers, and answers honestly, where the real poll had 53% who did neither; and that nobody changes their mind. What survives all four is the shape. Population size entered this poll's arithmetic once, through a term worth 0.0011%, and the error was 17.3 standard errors. Whatever went wrong here, the number of people interviewed was not it.
